title: TB Infection Testing: Mantoux Cutoffs, IGRA and BCG
summary: Place and read the tuberculin skin test, choose the 5, 10 or 15 mm cutoff by risk group, and see why BCG affects the skin test but not interferon-gamma release assays, plus who BCG protects and who must not receive it.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 59 Hit 2 (Mantoux dose, reading, cutoffs), Hit 3 (IGRA antigens and BCG), Hit 13 (BCG vaccine) and Exam Trap 3 (BCG does not cause a positive IGRA). Checked against Pai 2014 (read via a page-fetch tool), the ATS/IDSA/CDC 2017 guideline (Lewinsohn 2017; read via a page-fetch tool), CDC tuberculin skin test and BCG pages (read via a page-fetch tool), the WHO BCG page and the BCG World Atlas (Zwerling 2011). Qualifications: the reviewer’s cutoff lists are shorter than CDC’s (transplant and immunosuppression at 5 mm; mycobacteriology lab workers and children under 5 at 10 mm); Pai 2014 adds M. flavescens to the NTM that share ESAT-6/CFP-10; the BCG and cutoff rules are US guidance, whereas the 2011 BCG World Atlas lists the Philippines with a birth-dose BCG policy. Pai 2014 judges NTM a clinically unimportant cause of false-positive TSTs outside specific settings, so the lesson does not present NTM cross-reaction as routine. The reviewer’s description of BCG as “attenuated” M. bovis was not confirmed in the pages read; the lesson says only that BCG is derived from M. bovis. IGRA laboratory mechanics are taught in immuno-igra-t-cell-memory.

objectives: Describe how the tuberculin skin test is placed and read.
Choose the 5, 10 or 15 mm induration cutoff from a patient’s risk group.
Explain why BCG can cause a false-positive skin test but not a positive IGRA, and state who should not receive BCG.

scenes.title: Three arms, three readings
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three tuberculin skin tests are read at 48 hours. (1) A nurse born in a country where TB is common, vaccinated with BCG at birth: 12 mm induration. (2) A person with HIV who is a recent contact of an infectious TB case: 6 mm induration. (3) An office worker with no known TB risk factors: 12 mm induration. Question token: “Positive or not, and does BCG matter?”

cues.text: Three skin tests are read at forty-eight hours. A nurse born where tuberculosis is common, given BCG at birth, has twelve millimetres of induration.
A person with HIV, a recent contact of an infectious case, has six millimetres.
An office worker with no risk factors has twelve millimetres. Which are positive, and does the BCG matter?

props.label: Positive or not, and does BCG matter?

scenes.title: Placing and reading the skin test
scenes.altText: Schematic forearm. Card “Place”: 0.1 mL of tuberculin purified protein derivative (5 tuberculin units of PPD-S) injected intradermally on the inner forearm with a 27-gauge tuberculin syringe, bevel up; a pale wheal 6–10 mm across shows a correct intradermal injection; a wrong volume or a deep injection without a wheal means repeating at a site at least 2 inches away. Card “Reaction”: delayed-type hypersensitivity develops in 48–72 h. Card “Read”: a trained reader measures induration (not redness) across the forearm, perpendicular to its long axis, in millimetres.

cues.text: The tuberculin skin test injects zero point one millilitre of purified protein derivative, five tuberculin units of PPD-S, into the skin of the inner forearm.
A correct injection raises a pale wheal six to ten millimetres across. A wrong dose, or an injection too deep to raise a wheal, invalidates the test, which is repeated at a new site.
In a person sensitised to mycobacterial antigens, a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction develops within forty-eight to seventy-two hours.
A trained reader measures the induration, the firm swelling, across the forearm in millimetres. Redness is not measured.

props.title: Check the wheal
lines: No wheal or wrong dose: invalid, repeat

scenes.title: The cutoff depends on the person
scenes.altText: Three cutoff cards (CDC clinical testing guidance). ≥5 mm: people with HIV; recent contacts of infectious TB; chest radiograph findings suggestive of previous TB; organ transplant recipients; other immunosuppression such as prolonged corticosteroids (≥15 mg/day prednisone equivalent) or TNF-α antagonists. ≥10 mm: people born in countries where TB is common; people who misuse drugs or alcohol; residents and staff of high-risk congregate settings (nursing homes, homeless shelters, correctional facilities); mycobacteriology laboratory workers; conditions such as silicosis, diabetes, severe kidney disease, certain cancers; under 90% of ideal body weight; children under 5; children and adolescents exposed to high-risk adults. ≥15 mm: no known risk factors.

cues.text: The same induration means different things in different people. Five millimetres is positive in people with HIV, recent contacts of an infectious case, people whose chest film suggests previous tuberculosis, transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients.

Ten millimetres is positive for people born where tuberculosis is common, people who misuse drugs or alcohol, residents and staff of nursing homes, shelters and prisons, and mycobacteriology laboratory workers.
Ten millimetres also applies to diabetes, silicosis, severe kidney disease, certain cancers, low body weight, and children under five.
With no known risk factors, the cutoff is fifteen millimetres. Risk goes down, millimetres go up.

scenes.title: IGRA, BCG and the hook
scenes.altText: Card “IGRA antigens”: ESAT-6 and CFP-10 (encoded in the RD1 region of M. tuberculosis; QuantiFERON adds TB7.7) are not encoded in any BCG vaccine strain or most nontuberculous mycobacteria, except M. marinum, M. kansasii, M. szulgai and M. flavescens. QuantiFERON reports IFN-γ in IU/mL; T-SPOT.TB counts spot-forming cells. Neither IGRA nor TST separates latent from active TB. Card “BCG and the TST”: BCG can cause a false-positive TST, with no reliable way to tell it from infection; a single dose at birth has minimal effect on TST specificity, but vaccination after infancy or repeated doses compromise it; IGRA is preferred for BCG-vaccinated people aged 5 years or more, TST is suggested for healthy children under 5. Hook answers: (1) 12 mm, ≥10 mm group: positive whatever the BCG history, IGRA would be the preferred test; (2) 6 mm with HIV: positive; (3) 12 mm with no risk factors: below 15 mm, negative.

cues.text: Interferon-gamma release assays use ESAT-6 and CFP-10, antigens not encoded in any BCG strain and absent from most environmental mycobacteria, except marinum, kansasii, szulgai and flavescens.

BCG can make a skin test falsely positive, and nothing reliably separates that from infection. So guidelines prefer an IGRA for vaccinated people aged five or older. Neither test separates latent from active disease.
Back to the hook. The nurse belongs to the ten-millimetre group, so twelve millimetres is positive. The skin test is read by risk group, whatever the BCG history.
Six millimetres in the person with HIV is positive. Twelve millimetres with no risk factors is below fifteen: negative.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “BCG causes a positive IGRA” (✓ IGRA antigens are not encoded in BCG strains; it is the TST that BCG affects); “Measure the redness” (✓ measure induration only, in millimetres); “A positive IGRA or TST means active TB” (✓ neither test separates latent infection from active disease; active TB must be ruled out before treating latent infection).

cues.text: Trap one: BCG causes a positive IGRA. No: the IGRA antigens are not in any BCG strain. BCG affects the skin test.
Trap two: measure the redness. No: measure only the induration, in millimetres.
Trap three: a positive IGRA or skin test means active tuberculosis. No: neither test can tell latent infection from active disease.

props.title: ✗ “BCG makes the IGRA positive.”
lines: ✓ IGRA antigens are not in BCG; BCG affects the TST

props.title: ✗ “Positive test = active TB.”
lines: ✓ Neither test separates latent from active

scenes.title: Five, ten, fifteen
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “5-10-15: risk goes down, millimetres go up. IGRA ignores BCG.” Tokens: 5 = highest risk · 10 = other risk · 15 = no risk. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: five, ten, fifteen. Risk goes down, millimetres go up. And the IGRA ignores BCG.

Where it breaks: a few environmental mycobacteria share the IGRA antigens; BCG given after infancy or repeated affects the skin test more than a single birth dose; and the risk groups listed here are United States guidance.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: M. marinum, kansasii, szulgai, flavescens share IGRA antigens
Later or repeated BCG affects the TST more

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Read induration at 48–72 h · 5 / 10 / 15 mm by risk group”, “IGRA ignores BCG · neither test separates latent from active”.

cues.text: Read the skin test as induration at 48 to 72 hours against a 5, 10 or 15 millimetre cutoff chosen by risk group, and prefer an interferon-gamma release assay after BCG because its antigens are absent from every BCG strain.

props.label: Induration at 48–72 h · 5 / 10 / 15 mm by risk group
IGRA ignores BCG · neither test separates latent from active

explanation.what: Plain language: the skin test injects a small amount of tuberculosis protein into the skin; people whose immune system has met mycobacteria develop a firm bump in 2 to 3 days. How big a bump counts as positive depends on how likely the person is to have infection and to get sick. The blood test (IGRA) uses proteins that the BCG vaccine lacks, so the vaccine does not affect it. Scientific terms: tuberculin skin test (TST, Mantoux), purified protein derivative (PPD-S, 5 TU), intradermal wheal, delayed-type hypersensitivity, induration, interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), ESAT-6, CFP-10, TB7.7, region of difference 1 (RD1), bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG).
explanation.why: Prior BCG vaccination can make the TST falsely positive, especially when BCG is given after infancy or repeated; NTM infection can too, although Pai 2014 judges NTM a clinically unimportant cause outside specific settings. ESAT-6 and CFP-10 are not encoded in any BCG strain or most NTM, which makes IGRAs more specific than PPD in BCG-vaccinated people. CDC reads the TST against the person’s risk of TB infection or of progressing to TB disease if infected, so the cutoff changes with the risk group.
explanation.measure: TST: 0.1 mL PPD (5 TU PPD-S) intradermally, pale wheal 6–10 mm; read at 48–72 h; measure induration across the forearm in mm, not erythema. Cutoffs (CDC): ≥5 mm (HIV, recent contacts, chest film suggesting old TB, transplant, immunosuppression); ≥10 mm (born in high-TB countries, drug or alcohol misuse, high-risk congregate settings, mycobacteriology lab workers, diabetes, silicosis, severe kidney disease, certain cancers, under 90% ideal body weight, children under 5); ≥15 mm (no known risk factors). IGRA: QuantiFERON reports IFN-γ in IU/mL; T-SPOT.TB counts spot-forming cells.
explanation.differs: TST (PPD, can be falsely positive after BCG, two visits) vs IGRA (ESAT-6/CFP-10, not affected by BCG, fewer visits). Both detect immune sensitisation and neither separates latent infection from active TB. BCG at birth, not repeated, has minimal effect on TST specificity; BCG after infancy or repeated doses compromise it.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: classify a TST result from induration size and risk group, pick the test least affected by BCG, recognise that redness is not measured, and name who should not receive BCG (immunosuppressed, including HIV, and pregnant women).

right.label: IGRA

comparisons.distinguisher: Antigen choice: BCG can cause a positive PPD reaction, but BCG strains do not encode the RD1 antigens.

comparisons.title: BCG: who benefits, who must not receive it
comparisons.distinguisher: Benefit is mainly against severe childhood TB; immunosuppression and pregnancy are contraindications.

mnemonic.text: 5-10-15: risk goes down, millimetres go up. IGRA ignores BCG.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each TST cutoff to the risk group and reminds that BCG affects only the skin test.
mnemonic.limitation: M. marinum, M. kansasii, M. szulgai and M. flavescens share the IGRA antigens; BCG given after infancy or repeated affects the TST more than a single birth dose; the risk groups are US (CDC) guidance.

analogyLimitations: Cutoff groups follow US CDC guidance; other countries may differ.
takeaway: Read the skin test as induration at 48 to 72 hours against a 5, 10 or 15 millimetre cutoff chosen by risk group, and prefer an interferon-gamma release assay after BCG because its antigens are absent from every BCG strain.

questions.stem: A person with HIV who is a recent contact of an infectious tuberculosis case has 6 mm of induration 48 hours after a tuberculin skin test. How is the result interpreted?

options.text: Positive, because the cutoff for this person is 5 mm
options.rationale: Correct. People with HIV and recent contacts of infectious TB are positive at 5 mm or more.

options.text: Negative, because the cutoff is 10 mm
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 10 mm cutoff is for other risk groups, such as people born where TB is common or with diabetes.

options.text: Negative, because the cutoff is 15 mm
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 15 mm cutoff applies only to people with no known risk factors.

options.text: Invalid, because the test must be read at 96 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. The TST is read between 48 and 72 hours.

questions.stem: Why is an interferon-gamma release assay not made positive by prior BCG vaccination?

options.text: Its antigens, ESAT-6 and CFP-10, are not encoded in any BCG vaccine strain
options.rationale: Correct. These RD1 antigens are absent from BCG strains and most NTM.

options.text: It uses purified protein derivative at a lower dose than the skin test
options.rationale: Incorrect. PPD is the TST antigen and is shared with BCG.

options.text: BCG immunity has always faded by adulthood
options.rationale: Incorrect. The IGRA’s specificity comes from its antigens, which BCG strains do not encode, not from any assumption about BCG immunity fading.

options.text: It measures antibody rather than T-cell responses
options.rationale: Incorrect. IGRAs measure interferon-gamma released by sensitised T cells.

questions.stem: Which person should NOT receive BCG vaccine?

options.rationale: Correct. CDC states that pregnant women should not receive BCG; immunosuppressed people, including those with HIV, should not either.

options.text: A healthy newborn in a country with routine birth-dose BCG
options.rationale: Incorrect. BCG at birth is routine policy in many high-burden countries; the 2011 BCG World Atlas lists the Philippines with a birth-dose policy.

options.text: A child with a negative TB test who cannot be separated from an adult with untreated TB and cannot take preventive treatment
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is one of the limited situations in which CDC says BCG may be considered.

options.text: A health care worker where many patients have multidrug-resistant TB and full infection control has failed
options.rationale: Incorrect. CDC says BCG may be considered for such health care workers on an individual basis; it is not a contraindication.

claims.text: TST placement (0.1 mL, 5 TU PPD-S, intradermal, wheal 6–10 mm), reading at 48–72 h, induration not erythema.
IGRA antigens absent from BCG and most NTM (exceptions marinum, kansasii, szulgai, flavescens); QuantiFERON and T-SPOT.TB readouts; neither test separates latent from active TB.

BCG may cause a false-positive TST (NTM also can, but Pai 2014 calls NTM clinically unimportant outside specific settings); birth dose has minimal effect, later or repeated doses compromise specificity; IGRA preferred after BCG in people aged 5 or more; TST suggested in healthy children under 5.

BCG derived from M. bovis; protects children against TB meningitis and miliary TB; not generally used in the US; contraindicated in immunosuppression and pregnancy; may be considered for specific exposed children and, individually, for health care workers in high-MDR-TB settings; Philippines listed with a birth-dose policy in the 2011 BCG World Atlas.
Reviewer wording that BCG is an attenuated M. bovis strain.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 59 Hit 2 lists shorter cutoff groups than CDC guidance: CDC also places organ transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed people (prolonged corticosteroids, TNF-α antagonists) at ≥5 mm, and mycobacteriology laboratory workers, children under 5, silicosis, low body weight and high-risk congregate settings at ≥10 mm (register flag rv-tst-cutoff-groups).
Ch. 59 Hit 3 lists M. kansasii, M. szulgai and M. marinum as the NTM exceptions and Exam Trap 3 calls them the only ones; Pai 2014 also lists M. flavescens (register flag rv-igra-ntm-flavescens).

The TST cutoff groups and the statement that BCG is not used routinely are US (CDC/ATS/IDSA) guidance. The BCG World Atlas (2011) lists the Philippines with a BCG-at-birth policy; Philippine TB-testing rules are not covered (register flag rv-tst-bcg-us-guideline).
